13_marg737: RABANUS. It is read, or it is written: they declare that this book is found nowhere, like the book of the wars of the Lord, of which mention is made in the book of Numbers, and the songs of Solomon and his discourses on the nature of trees, herbs, beasts, birds, creeping things and fishes. Or what is said in the book of the Chronicles: "Now the rest of the acts of Solomon, first and last, are written in the books of Nathan the prophet, and of Ahias the Silonite, and in the vision of Addo the seer against Jeroboam the son of Nabat," and many volumes of this kind, which it proves were written but which it is certain do not exist today. For when Judea was laid waste by the Chaldeans, the library was consumed by the enemy's fire. But a few books were repaired or restored by Esdras the high priest, through the diligence of prophecy. This Esdras was a scribe in the law of God, who devised readier shapes of letters than the Hebrews had had until then. And there are some who say that the Book of the Just is the Book of Kings, in which are contained the just prophets Samuel, Gad and Nathan, in which it is written how Saul, departing from the fear of the Lord, perished through disobedience.

13_marg742: David, king and prophet, who did not return evil to his persecutors, when Saul and Jonathan had fallen in battle, cursed the mountains of Gelboe in his lamentation: Ye mountains of Gelboe, let neither dew nor rain etc. What fault did the mountains commit? But because Gelboe is interpreted 'a running down', and through Saul, anointed and dead, the anointing and death of our mediator is expressed, by Gelboe are fittingly signified the proud hearts of the Jews, which, while they flow away in the desires of this world, mixed themselves in the death of the anointed, that is, of Christ. And because in them the anointed king dies in time, they are dried up from all dew of grace. Of them it is said that they cannot be fields of firstfruits. For the proud mountains of the Hebrews do not bear the first fruits, since at the Redeemer's coming they for the most part remained in unbelief and would not follow the beginnings of the faith. For holy Church, made fruitful in her firstfruits by the multitude of the gentiles, scarcely at the end of the world receives the Jews whom she finds, and gathering the last ones lays them up as the remnants of the harvest. Whence: THE REMNANT OF ISRAEL SHALL BE SAVED. Yet the mountains of Gelboe can be cursed by the prophet's mouth, so that, while the fruit dies as the earth dries up, the possessors of the land might be struck with the loss of barrenness, that they themselves might receive the sentence of the curse who, as their iniquity required, had deserved to have the death of the king take place among them.
13_marg743: Blood and fat give strength to the body. So those by whom Saul and Jonathan were slain gave strength to their subjects, as though [they had been slain] not by rustics. 13_marg744: THE ARROW OF JONATHAN etc. and THE SWORD OF SAUL etc. He shows that Jonathan and Saul were warlike and most valiant, and praises in them the comeliness of their form and the constancy of their mind.
13_marg745: Allegorically. First the prophet David figuratively bewails Saul and Jonathan, who, though they were mighty and always prevailed over their enemies, being wounded and struck down in the midst of the battle, fell. So also Christians bewail those who, fighting against the demons, slip in the slipperiness of the world (for Gelboe is interpreted 'slippery mountains'), and, giving up the hope of recovery, kill themselves with their own blade of despair, as Saul did falling upon his sword. But the Philistines, that is, the demons, carrying off the spoils of virtues from the slain, ascribe the victory to their own strength, since such things befall the just by the promise of God. But our David in his elect groans at the fall of those who fall, and forbids it to be published in the cities of the aliens, that is, he commands the faithful to guard themselves warily, that they may have the shield of faith, the breastplate of justice, the helmet of salvation, and the sword of the spirit, which is the word of God, with which they may resist their adversaries, lest, shamefully overcome again, they give joy to their enemies.

13_marg751: RABANUS. It is well said that David reigned seven days [so the edition] and six months in Hebron, which is interpreted 'marriage' or 'everlasting vision', because Christ reigns in the Church, which is his person, through the whole time of this life, which runs its course in the sevenfold number of days, according to that: "Behold I am with you all days, even to the consummation of the world"; and because after the fulfilment of the six, that is, the perfection of good work, he leads his elect to the true sabbath, that is, the everlasting rest, where they shall enjoy the perpetual vision of God. Now Hebron is a city in the tribe of Juda which was once called Arbe, although in the Greek manuscripts it is wrongly given as Arboc, as also in ours, whereas in the Hebrew it is read Arbe, that is, 'four', because Abraham and Isaac and Jacob were buried there, and the great Adam, although some suppose he [was buried] in the place of Calvary. This was once the metropolis of the Philistines and the dwelling of the giants, afterwards a priestly city and [a city] of refuge. It lies on the southern side, about twenty-two miles from Aelia, where the oak of Abraham, which is also the terebinth, which is also Mambre, was shown until the reign of the emperor Constantine, and his mausoleum [is seen] at the present time. And though a church has now been built there by our people, the place of the terebinth is worshipped round about by all the nations with superstition, because under it Abraham received the angels as guests. It was first called Arbe, afterwards Hebron, from one of the sons of Caleb; and it was founded seven years before Tanis, the city of Egypt.
13_marg752: AND ABNER WENT OUT etc. RABANUS. Josephus explains this passage thus: Abner moved forward a very choice army, to engage with the tribe of Juda. For he was angry against those by whom David had been ordained king. Against him came Joab, sent by David, the son of Sarvia his sister; he was set as captain of the host against Abner. With him were his brothers Abisai and Asael and all David's armed men; and coming to a certain spring in the city of Gabaon, he drew up his line for battle. And when Abner said to him that he wished to test which of them had the stronger army, it was agreed between both that they should send twelve men to fight; and when the swords were drawn, David's men, holding the heads of the enemy, pierced their loins and sides with their swords, until all perished as if in one appointed danger. When these fell, the rest of the army also gave way, and Abner's people were beaten. And Joab did not cease to pursue the fleeing, commanding the armed men to hasten and not to slacken in killing. His brothers also fought most readily; among whom Asael was the more renowned, who had such glory in swiftness of foot that he outran even horses in running. He pursued Abner, turning aside to neither side.
13_marg753: AND ABNER SAID TO JOAB etc. Abner, of the tribe of Benjamin, captain of Saul's army, provoked the young men of David to battle; and Saul, not yet an apostle, of the tribe of Benjamin, a Pharisee, provoked the apostles to the contest, and was present at the killing of Stephen.
13_marg754: NOW ASAEL etc. GREGORY. Asael signifies those whom vehement fury seizes and drives headlong. They are to be avoided the more cautiously in that same onset of fury, the more madly they are carried away. Whence Abner, that is, 'lamp of the father', flees, because the tongue of teachers, which shows forth the heavenly light of God, when it sees anyone's mind carried along the steep places of fury, refrains from returning the darts of words against the angry man, as if unwilling to strike the pursuer. But when the wrathful are mitigated by no consideration, and like Asael do not cease to pursue, it is necessary that those who try to restrain the furious should not rouse themselves to fury, but show whatever there is of calm; and some things they should put forward subtly, by which they may obliquely pierce the mind of the furious man. Whence Abner pierced his pursuer not with the point but with the butt of the spear. For to strike with the point is to oppose with the onset of open rebuke; but to strike with the butt of the spear is to touch the furious man calmly with certain things, and as it were to overcome him by sparing him. And Asael at once falls, because agitated minds, when they both feel themselves spared and yet are touched inwardly, under calm, by the reason of the answers, immediately fall from that to which they had raised themselves. Because, therefore, struck by gentleness they spring back from the onset of their fury, they die as it were without the steel.

13_marg759: ABNER ALSO SPOKE. RABANUS. Abner exhorts all Israel to leave Isboseth the son of Saul and come over to David, because the holy teachers, who are called lamp of the father, full of the light of faith and knowledge, exhort all nations to spurn the worship of idols, to leave the error of confusion together with its author the devil, and to hasten to come to the true David, that is, Christ. For Joab too, who, speaking to Abner in guile, struck him in the groin and killed him, signifies the ancient enemy, who subverts the faithful by fraud and kills them through the contagion of lust. For Joab is interpreted 'enemy' or likewise 'father'. For the devil is the head of all the wicked. Whence: "You are of your father the devil." Of this killing David is guiltless, because "God tempteth no man," who "will have all men to be saved." "But by the envy of the devil death came into the world." The person and name of Joab can also signify the people of the Jews, who were always enemies of the preachers and persecuted the faith of Christ everywhere.

13_marg765: RABANUS. The doorkeeper cleanses wheat when the guard of the mind, by discerning, separates virtues from vices; and if she falls asleep, she admits the plotters to the death of her own lord, because when the care of discretion has ceased, it opens the way to the evil spirits to kill the soul. They, entering, take away the ears of corn, because they carry off the seeds of good thoughts, and they strike in the groin, because they kill the strength of the heart with the delight of the flesh. For to strike in the groin is to pierce the life of the mind with the delight of the flesh. For Isboseth would not have fallen by an unforeseen death if he had not set a woman at the entrance of the house, that is, a soft guard at the approach of the mind. For a strong and wakeful sense ought to be set before the doors of the heart, which neither the sleep of negligence may overpower nor the error of ignorance deceive. Whence he is fitly called Isboseth who, with a woman as guard, is laid bare to the swords of the enemy. For Isboseth is called man of confusion. And the man of confusion is he who is not fortified with a strong guard of the mind, because while he thinks he is practising virtues, the vices creeping in kill him unawares. With all strength, therefore, the approach of the mind must be fortified, lest the enemies pierce it through the opening of a neglected thought.

13_marg769: RABANUS. It is asked why forty years and six months are not counted in the sum. This is resolved by the Hebrews in two ways. For they say that David fled from his son Absalom for six months, and these were subtracted from the sum of his reign. They say also that for six months in Hebron he laboured under bodily infirmity, and therefore these ought not to be counted. For they say that he reigned in Hebron from the time when, having conquered the Amalecites, he sent presents from their spoils to the ancients of Juda, namely those who were in Hebron and in Bethel and wherever David had stayed. And that David began to reign at thirty years signifies that our Lord, when he was thirty years old, came to baptism and began to preach the gospel of the kingdom, whose kingdom is everlasting and his power eternal. And the number forty, which consists of four tens, signifies the perfection of times and things.

13_marg773: RABANUS. David, casting out of Jerusalem the Jebusite, the inhabitant of the land, signifies Christ casting the opposing powers out of the hearts of the faithful and abiding there. Whence: "Behold, I have given you power to tread upon serpents and scorpions" etc. Fittingly, then, David, the blind and the lame being cast out, dwelt in the castle of Sion and named it his city, because when Christ has driven the evil spirits and the crowd of vices out of the soul, he dwells there. And it is rightly called the castle of Sion, that is, 'of watching', that it may rightly be said of it: "His place is in peace, and his abode in Sion: there hath he broken the bow, the shield, the sword, and the battle."

13_marg783: AND DAVID AGAIN GATHERED etc. David [signifies] Christ, the ark signifies the Church. David sought to bring the ark into his city, but, a cause intervening, he turned it aside elsewhere for a time and afterwards fulfilled what he had vowed; because the Lord, appearing in the flesh, preached the gospel to his own nation, but "blindness in part has happened in Israel, until the fulness of the gentiles should come in, and so all Israel should be saved." David gathered thirty thousand chosen men out of Israel, because the Lord established the primitive Church out of Israel, associating to himself not all but the chosen; "for not all that are of Israel are Israelites, but the children of the promission are accounted for the seed." They are called thirty thousand, that is, perfect in the firmness of faith, work and hope. For three, on account of the confession of the Trinity, pertains to faith; ten, on account of the decalogue, to works; a thousand, on account of its perfection, to the hope of eternal life, than which nothing is higher, as no number is greater than a thousand. For if thou sayest ten thousand, or thirty, or even a thousand thousand, thou dost not go beyond the thousand itself in counting, but multiplyest it, either by itself or by leading it more often through smaller numbers. Multiply three, then, by ten, lest "faith without works be dead"; likewise thirty by a thousand, that faith which worketh by charity may hope for its reward nowhere but in heaven. The chosen out of Israel, then, signify 'peoples rightly believing, working and hoping'. And the men of Juda who were with David signify 'the apostles and teachers', clinging as it were more familiarly to Christ's side; attended by these the Lord rejoices to bring the ark, that is, to enlarge the Church and to set it in the hearts of those who had not believed. The ark is set upon a new cart, that the grace of the new Testament may be poured into those renewed in baptism, and "new wine" be entrusted "to new bottles." The ark was indeed first in the house of Aminadab, who was in Gabaa, because the same faith which the preacher of the Church now [proclaims] flourished also before the time of the Lord's incarnation in those who followed the devotion of the patriarchs. For Aminadab, who is interpreted 'my God willing', signifies either 'Abraham the father of faith' or 'Moses the lawgiver', each of whom keeps the ark in Gabaa, because by a lofty example of virtue he fortifies the breasts of believers. Whence Gabaa too is interpreted 'hill', which is a place in the city of Cariathiarim. When the ark was brought out, David and all Israel played before the Lord with various instruments and kinds of musicians, because, as the proclamation of the new grace begins, the Lord invites all to render praises of humility to God the Father, saying: "If any man minister to me, let him follow me"; "to one is given by the Spirit the word of wisdom, to another the word of knowledge, to another divers kinds of tongues" etc. But as the ark advanced with these and such kinds of gifts, that is, as the primitive Church grew, they came to the floor of Nachor, that is, the floor prepared in the Church of the gentiles to be consecrated by the truth of faith, of which it is said: "He will thoroughly cleanse his floor," where the priest who incautiously touched the ark, as if to correct it, soon fell struck by the Lord; because the people of the Jews, while it envies the gentiles, is deprived of the gift of salvation. While it wishes to mix the law with the gospel, it loses the grace of both. He held it because the oxen kicked. For the oxen to kick is for 'the preachers of the gospel' to act more freely concerning the faith, and not to walk according to the custom of the law, but to interpret the sabbaths, new moons, circumcision and victims spiritually. These, as if erring, they tried to correct who, coming down from Judea, taught the brethren: "Except you be circumcised after the manner of Moses, you cannot be saved."

13_marg785: GREGORY. In the history of David, king and prophet, in which he is said to have brought the ark of God, humility is shown approved, pride condemned and rashness punished. For David, who was not ashamed to dance humbly before the ark, soon deserved to receive the promise of the Son of God to be born of his stock; and the wife who despised his humility paid the penalty of perpetual barrenness. The priest also who rashly touched the ark purged the guilt of his daring by an untimely death. Here it is to be considered how greatly he sins who approaches the body of the Lord guilty, if he is punished with death who laid hold of the ark, the figure of the Lord's body, with less veneration than he ought.
13_marg786: Often, because they cannot be understood, the deeds or words of the better displease the worse. But they ought the less rashly to be blamed by them, the less they can be truly grasped. Often something is done by the greater by way of dispensation which is thought an error by the lesser. Often many things are said by the strong which the weak judge, because they do not understand them. This is well signified by that ark of the testament tilted by the kicking oxen, which the Levite, believing it would fall, wished to raise, and soon received the sentence of death. For what is the mind of the just man but the ark of the testament, which is tilted by the kicking oxen, because often even he who rules well, while he is shaken by compassion for his subjects, is moved from love alone to the condescension of dispensation. But in this, which is done by dispensation, the tilting of strength is thought a fall by the unskilled. Whence the subjects also put forth the hand of reproof against it, but by their very rashness they forthwith fail from life. The Levite, then, stretched out his hand as if helping, but by sinning lost his life, because when the weak reprove the deeds of the strong, they are rejected from the very lot of the living. Sometimes holy men say certain things condescending to the least, and put forth certain things contemplating the highest; and while the foolish do not know the force either of the condescension or of the height, they boldly blame these. And what is it to wish to correct a just man for his condescension, but to raise the tilted ark with the proud hand of reproof? What is it to blame a just man for speech not understood, but to think the movement of his strength the lapse of error? But he loses his life who proudly lifts up the ark of God, because no one presumes to correct the right things of the saints unless he first thinks better things of himself. Whence the Levite also is called Oza, that is, 'strong of the Lord', because the presumptuous, unless they believed themselves strong in the Lord, would not judge the deeds or words of the better as weak.

13_marg787: WHO DIED THERE etc. When the priest had died, he did not dare to turn the ark aside to himself into the city of David, but turned it aside into the house of Obededom the Gethite; because, when the Jews rejected the word, lest the preaching heard and not received should harm them the more, the apostles passed over to the gentiles. Whence the place of the floor of Nachor, which signifies 'the faith of the gentiles prepared for the grace of the Lord', is named the striking of Oza, because by their offence salvation came to the gentiles. For Obededom, who is interpreted 'a serving man', signifies him of whom it is said: "A people which I knew not hath served me: at the hearing of the ear" etc.; and, as it were, the death of Oza is set before it: "Thou wilt deliver me from the contradictions of the people." Geth also is interpreted 'winepress', signifying 'the cross', on which the true vine deigned to be trodden and pressed. From which the people can be called Gethite that says: "But God forbid that I should glory, save in the cross of the Lord."

13_marg791: AND WHEN THE ARK OF THE LORD WAS COME INTO THE CITY etc. While all rejoice and sound hymns at the entrance of the heavenly ark, Michol the daughter of Saul alone is absent, and from the spectacle despises David humbled; because, when the Jews believe at the end of the world, many will follow Christ in profession but Antichrist in deed. To them it fits that Michol (who, to figure 'the instability of the carnal', is interpreted 'all water') is called not the wife of David but the daughter of Saul, because those who serve Christ as far as faith [only] are not to be crowned in his kingdom, but to be condemned with the anathema of his persecutors, whom they imitate. But though the wicked be angry and despise the humility of the Church, nonetheless the ark of the Lord enters its place and is set in the midst of the tabernacle which David had pitched for it; that is, the faith of the Church is preached, advances, and is set in the hearts of all whom God has foreordained to eternal life. David offers holocausts and peace offerings before the Lord: Christ commends the faith and devotion of the Church to the Father, he who "is at the right hand of God, who also maketh intercession for us"; who, after the example of David, blessing the faithful and humble, feeds them with the food of the saving mystery. He distributes to each one cake of bread, namely of him who "cometh down from heaven, and giveth life to the world"; and one piece of roasted beef, namely of that fatted calf which was slain for the returning son and roasted in the fire of the passion, saying: "My strength is dried up like a potsherd"; and fine flour fried with oil, namely the flesh most pure from the stain of sin, but, for the sake of human salvation, most rich in delights, cooked in the frying pan of the cross. Fittingly one cake of one bread [and] one piece of roasted flesh is given, because there is "one Lord, one faith, one baptism, one God and Father" almighty. Otherwise: the faithful receive these gifts when, many being one bread and one body in Christ, each of them chastises the wantonness of his flesh and brings it into subjection. They cook [it] in the fire of the Spirit, and make the fruits of good works, most rich with the oil of mercy, to seethe with compassion for their neighbour. But on the contrary the daughter of Saul, having entered the king's chamber, gives no fruit of conceived seed, because those who receive the word of God with the ear only await the day of perpetual death without the offspring of good work.

13_marg792: AND MICHOL THE DAUGHTER OF SAUL CAME OUT etc. GREGORY. It is good to consider what great gifts of virtues David had received, and in all these how strong he kept himself by humility. For whom would it not lift up to break the jaws of lions, to tear apart the arms of bears, to be chosen when his elder brothers were passed over, to be anointed to the government of the kingdom when the king was rejected, to lay low with one stone Goliath, feared by all, to bring back the numerous foreskins proposed by the king when the aliens were slain, to receive at length the promised kingdom, and to possess the whole people of Israel without any gainsaying? And yet, when he brings the ark of God back into Jerusalem, as if forgetting that he was set over all, mingled with the people he dances before the ark. And because to dance before the ark had been (as is believed) the custom of the common people, the king whirls himself in the dance in divine service. Behold, he whom the Lord preferred singularly to all makes himself equal to the least beneath the Lord and despises himself by showing himself abject. The power of the kingdom is not called to mind; he does not fear to grow vile by dancing in the eyes of his subjects; he does not acknowledge himself set in honour above the rest before the ark of him who had given the honour. Before God he did weak or the lowest things, that by humility he might make firm those brave things which he had done before men. What others think of these deeds I do not know; I am more amazed at David dancing than fighting. By fighting he subdued the enemy; by dancing before the Lord he conquered himself. When Michol, the daughter of Saul, still mad with the swelling of royal birth, despised him humbled, saying: How glorious was the king today, uncovering himself before the handmaids of his servants, and was naked, as if one of the buffoons, she forthwith heard: I will play before the Lord, who chose me rather than thy father; and a little after: I will both play and make myself meaner than I have done, and I will be humble in my own eyes. As if he should say: I seek to be vile before men, because I seek to keep my nobility before God through humility. There are some who think humbly of themselves, who, placed in honours, weigh themselves as nothing but dust and ashes, but shrink from appearing vile before men, and, against what they think of themselves within, cloak themselves outwardly as it were with a stiff comeliness. And there are some who desire to be seen as vile by men, and despise all that they are by showing themselves cast down, but within themselves swell as if from the very merit of the vileness they have shown, and are the more lifted up in heart the more they press down elation in appearance. Both these wars of elation David detected with great circumspection and overcame with wonderful virtue. For that, thinking humbly of himself within, he does not seek honour outwardly, he intimates by saying: I will play and make myself meaner. And because through showing himself vile outwardly he does not swell inwardly, he adds: and I will be humble in my own eyes; as if he should say: such as I show myself outwardly, such I regard myself inwardly. What then will they do whom learning lifts up, if David, who knew that the Redeemer would come of his flesh and announced his joys by prophesying, nevertheless pressed down in himself the neck of the heart with the strong heel of discretion, saying: and I will be humble in my own eyes?
13_marg793: GLORIOUS etc. David, when he brought the ark over into Jerusalem, was mocked by Michol. And Christ, when he brought the New Testament over into his Church, was a mockery to the Jews on the cross; he appeared naked while, hiding his power from them, he showed the infirmity of the flesh as a linen ephod. The handmaids of the servants bear the person of the saints, among whom he was made more glorious through the triumph of the cross; and while Michol mocks him, he appears more glorious to the handmaids, while she, in the type of the Synagogue, remained barren.

13_marg795: It is plain that the Spirit of prophecy does not always shine upon the minds of the prophets: "For the Spirit breatheth where he will." Hence Eliseus says: "The Lord hath hid it from me, and hath not told me." Which God orders by a dispensation of mercy, because while he gives and withdraws the Spirit of prophecy, he both lifts up the minds of the prophets to the heights and keeps them in humility, that, receiving the Spirit, they may find what they are from God, and again, not having the Spirit of prophecy, they may know what they are of themselves.
13_marg796: He who takes care to correct others ought to be clean of vices in himself, that he may not think on earthly things, that he may not yield to the lowest desires, so that he may see the more clearly what others must flee, the more truly he himself avoids these through knowledge and life. The eye which dust weighs down does not see clearly a blemish in a limb, and hands that hold mud cannot wipe away the filth laid upon [something]. Which, according to the ancient translation, is well said by way of signification to David, labouring in outward wars: "Thou shalt not build me a temple, because thou art a man of blood." He builds the temple of God who gives himself to correcting and instructing the minds of his neighbours. We are the temple of God, who are built up for the true life by his indwelling. Whence: "The temple of God is holy, which you are." But the man of blood is forbidden to build the temple of God, because he who still lies upon carnal acts must needs be ashamed to instruct the minds of his neighbours.

13_marg799: This is truly said of Christ. For the house of Solomon was full of foreign women worshipping false gods and driving Solomon himself to the same. But in Christ these things are fulfilled, who is "of the seed of David according to the flesh." The Jews understand the son of David promised in this place to be Solomon, and still, with wonderful blindness, say that they hope for another. There was indeed another image of the thing to come in Solomon, because he built the temple and had peace according to his name; for Solomon is interpreted 'peaceable'. At the beginning of his reign he was praiseworthy, but he foretold Christ, he did not show him; whence certain things are written of him as though foretold of [Christ] himself, while Scripture paints in him the figure of things to come. For in the Psalm which is entitled with his name many things are said which cannot fit him, but evidently fit Christ: for in Solomon is the figure, in Christ the truth. For it is known within what bounds the kingdom of Solomon was enclosed, whereas there it is read: "He shall rule from sea to sea, and from the river unto the ends of the earth." But Christ took the beginning of his rule from the river, where, baptized by John and pointed out by him, he began to be acknowledged by the disciples, who called him not only master but also Lord. Nor did he begin to reign while his father was still living (which befell none of those kings) for any other reason than that it might appear that he is not the one whom the prophecy foreshows, saying: When thy days shall be fulfilled and thou shalt sleep with thy fathers, I will raise up thy seed after thee etc. For this is the true peaceable one, who is prophesied to be raised up not before, as Solomon was, but after the death of David; who built a house to God not of wood and stones but of men. Whence: "The temple of God is holy, which you are." For the blessing of the Lord upon the seed of David is to be hoped for for ever; whence with most certain hope it is said, so be it, so be it, according to that: "Blessed be the Lord for evermore. So be it. So be it." And the repetition itself is the confirmation of hope. Whence David: "And thou hast spoken also of the house of thy servant for a long time to come." Then he added: "Now begin, and bless the house of thy servant for ever," because then he was to beget a son, from whom his progeny would be reckoned to Christ. Therefore, since according to the Seventy it was said in the words of Nathan: "And the Lord will tell thee that thou shalt build a house for him," afterwards David himself says: "Because thou, O Lord God almighty, God of Israel, hast revealed to the ear of thy servant, saying: I will build thee a house." For this house we build by living well, and God by helping. When the last dedication of this house shall come, that will be fulfilled which was said by Nathan: "And I will appoint a place for my people Israel, and I will plant them, and they shall dwell apart, and shall be troubled no more; and the son of iniquity shall not afflict them any more, as from the beginning, from the days when I appointed judges over my people Israel." For there were judges before there were kings, and the son of iniquity, that is, the foreign enemy, afflicted the people at intervals of time; and periods of peace are found there longer than Solomon had, who reigned forty years. For under the judge Aod, the son of iniquity [having] afflicted the people, there was peace for eighty years. These things, then, were not promised under Solomon, nor did any of those kings reign in such peace that that nation was not troubled. The place of so peaceful and secure a dwelling, then, is eternal, where there will be the true Israel, that is, seeing God.
